planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, average to rocky soil in partial shade to full sun; Alabama croton is a rare, disjunct native shrub of a few Alabama river-bluff counties and a separate Texas Hill Country population, and is notably drought-tolerant once established on well-drained slopes.

directions: Plant container shrubs in well-drained, average to rocky soil in partial shade to full sun. Alabama croton is a distinctive deciduous native shrub known from only a handful of dolomite bluff sites in central Alabama and a separate disjunct population in the Texas Hill Country, prized in cultivation for its silvery, metallic-scaled leaf undersides that shimmer in a breeze and its coppery orange-bronze fall color, which often persists as attractive winter foliage before finally dropping. Small, inconspicuous yellowish flowers appear in early spring, but the plant's real value is architectural and textural, forming a multi-stemmed, upright thicket useful as a specimen or informal screen. Its native rocky-bluff habitat makes it genuinely drought-tolerant and adaptable to lean, well-drained soils once established, an unusual trait among native shade shrubs, though it still benefits from watering through its first year or two. A rewarding, low-maintenance rarity for a native plant collector's garden.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full shade; croomia is a rare ravine-forest endemic of Alabama, the Florida Panhandle, and southwest Georgia, spreading slowly by rhizome to form a low colony in deep shade.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated rhizome divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full shade. Croomia is a rare, slow-spreading rhizomatous perennial known from only a scattering of rich, shaded ravine and bluff forests in Alabama, the Florida Panhandle, and southwest Georgia, forming a low colony of glossy, broadly veined leaves close to the ground beneath a hardwood canopy. Small, inconspicuous maroon flowers are produced close to the soil in spring, largely hidden beneath the foliage and easy to miss, but the real appeal of the plant is its handsome, deep-shade-tolerant foliage, which forms an attractive, slowly spreading groundcover where few other plants will grow. Because natural populations are limited and geographically restricted, source only nursery-propagated divisions, and site the planting in the deepest, most consistently moist, humus-rich shade available, mimicking the ravine-forest floor it calls home.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in spring in wet, acidic, nutrient-poor peaty or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade; Carolina bogmint grows naturally in the same wet pine savannas and seepage bogs as pitcher plants along the South Carolina, Georgia, and Florida Panhandle coastal plain.

directions: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in wet, acidic, nutrient-poor peaty or sandy soil in full sun to partial shade. Carolina bogmint is a showy member of the mint family native to wet pine savannas and seepage bogs of the South Carolina, Georgia, and Florida Panhandle coastal plain, producing dense, rounded heads of pink-purple, two-lipped flowers in summer that stand out against the low, grassy texture of a typical bog garden planting. It grows in the same nutrient-poor, consistently wet, acidic ground favored by pitcher plants and orchids, making it a natural companion plant that adds late-summer color once the spring pitcher plant flowers have faded. Keep the soil constantly moist to wet and avoid fertilizing, since like its bog neighbors it is adapted to low-nutrient conditions and rich garden soil favors weeds over this specialized wetland native. Established clumps slowly spread by rhizome in a favorable bog garden setting.
